aboutH2: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre: Early Recovery for Men in Kitamaat Village
intro: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre Society is a non-profit residential addiction treatment centre in Kitamaat Village, on the traditional unceded territory of the Haisla Nation on BC's northwest coast. Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab means healing each other in the x̄á’isla language. The centre runs one program, the Early Recovery and Stabilization Addictions Program, for adult men 19 and older.

The program is built for the start of recovery. It accepts men who are still "wet" and in minor withdrawal, men on methadone or Suboxone, and mandated clients, which removes some of the barriers other programs set. The centre focuses on the first two years of recovery and says it meets people where they are, whether they are still thinking about change or already making it.

pillars.title: A Small Centre on Haisla Nation Territory
pillars.body: The centre sits in Kitamaat Village, the Haisla community at the head of Douglas Channel, a short drive from the town of Kitimat. It carries a Haisla name and acknowledges that it operates on the traditional unceded territory of the Haisla Nation. With 13 beds, intakes stay small on purpose, and the centre says that keeps the program safe and manageable. Staff cover daily care, meals, maintenance and overnight presence, so someone is always in the building.

pillars.title: Planning for Home Is Part of the Program
pillars.body: Before you are accepted, you line up a referral worker or counsellor who will support you both before and after treatment, and the last week of the 8-week program is set aside for reflection, closure and planning. An Aftercare Coordinator works on the team. Employment readiness, life skills and diabetes and health sessions are there to help with ordinary life back home, and the module on post-acute withdrawal (PAWS) prepares men for the months after they leave.

pillars.title: Counsellors, Elders and Wellness Practitioners
pillars.body: Executive Director Lorraine Stewart leads the centre, with Jennifer Forde as Director of Clinical Services and Rigo Soriano as Head Counsellor and Facilitator. Two Elders, Clifford Smith and Sylvia Wilson, provide cultural support. A naturopathic physician and an attending physician are part of the care team, and practitioners offer reflexology, expressive arts therapy, tapping and relaxation. The centre says it trains and hires local staff, including people without formal education, to build skills in the community.

overviewH2: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre: Programs Overview
overview: The Early Recovery and Stabilization Addictions Program uses what the centre calls a Bio-Psycho-Social approach. In practice that means looking at physical health, emotions, relationships and daily life together, and starting from wherever each man is. The centre describes its care as trauma informed and client centred. Its motto is "clients first, last, and always", and it says the program has changed over time in response to client feedback.
serviceCaption: 12 services · as described by the centre
afterOverview: The program is modular. A man can join a full 6, 7, 8 or 12-week residential cycle, stay for only the modules that fit his needs, or come as a day patient for single modules or the full program. The centre accepts clients who are in minor withdrawal and people on methadone or Suboxone, and it can request detox if staff feel it is necessary. Cultural approaches are offered next to the clinical work, and the centre says they are guided by respect, inclusion and individual choice.

location.heading: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre in Kitamaat Village, British Columbia
location.intro: The centre is in Kitamaat Village, the Haisla community at the head of Douglas Channel in Northern BC, about 15 minutes by road from Kitimat. From Vancouver it is roughly 16 hours by road, so most people fly to the Northwest Regional Airport in Terrace, about an hour away; Prince Rupert is about 2.5 hours, Smithers about 3 hours and Prince George about 7.5 hours.

faqIntro: Answers come from the centre's own website and public listings. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: Who can attend Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre?
faqs.a: The program is for adult men aged 19 and older who are in early recovery from substance use. The centre says participants come from both Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities, and each admission is assessed on its own to make sure the program is a safe fit. It welcomes mandated clients and men with addiction-related convictions, except sexual assault convictions, and takes no more than 3 clients with parole, probation or bail orders per intake.

faqs.q: What type of treatment does the centre offer?
faqs.a: It runs one residential program, the Early Recovery and Stabilization Addictions Program, for men in the first stage of recovery. The program is modular: you can stay for a full 6, 7, 8 or 12-week cycle, stay for 1 to 8 modules, or attend as a day patient. It mixes alcohol and drug counselling, mental health counselling, psychoeducational groups and cultural practices with support from a naturopathic physician.

faqs.q: How long is the program, and when are the intakes?
faqs.a: Cycles run 6, 7, 8 or 12 weeks. The centre lists five intakes for 2026: a 12-week program from January 5, 7-week programs from April 6 and October 19, and 8-week programs from May 25 and August 17. Graduations are on Wednesdays at 2 pm so men travelling by public transit have Thursday and Friday to get home.

faqs.q: How much does it cost, and how is it funded?
faqs.a: The centre does not publish a fee. Its website says it runs 8 beds funded through the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program (NNADAP) and 5 beds funded by Northern Health. The referral package it posts is the shared package for FNHA-funded treatment centres, and it asks that funding (for example corrections, an employer, FNHA, yourself or your band) and travel funding be in place before you attend. Ask the intake worker what applies to you.

faqs.q: Does Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab offer detox?
faqs.a: It is not a medical detox centre, but it does accept men who are still "wet" and in minor withdrawal from their drug of choice. A naturopathic physician on the care team helps with withdrawal support, and the centre says it can request detox if staff feel it is needed.

faqs.q: Can I attend if I am on methadone or Suboxone?
faqs.a: Yes. The centre welcomes people on opioid agonist treatment, including methadone and Suboxone, and lists methadone maintenance clients as eligible. Bring your prescription details into the intake package so the medical section is complete.

Start by finding a referral worker or counsellor who will support you before and after treatment, then complete the intake package together. You also need a medical exam and a TB test, with your physician filling in the medical section, and the package goes to the centre by fax or email. A review panel of three program counsellors decides on fit, and the cut-off is 2 Wednesdays at 2 pm before the intake date.

The centre names three common reasons: incomplete intake or medical forms, literacy concerns (the program needs Grade 8 reading and writing), and missing legal paperwork such as bail, probation or parole orders, upcoming court dates or the nature of charges. Approved files are waitlisted when an intake is full.

faqs.q: Is culture part of the program?
faqs.a: Yes. Elders are on staff, and the centre says cultural and spiritual practices, including traditional ceremonies and spiritual teachings, run through the program. It also says cultural approaches are offered alongside clinical care and are guided by respect and individual choice. The name Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab means healing each other in the x̄á’isla language.

faqs.q: Where is the centre and how do I get there?
faqs.a: The centre is at 322H Haisla Ave in Kitamaat Village, on Haisla Nation territory at the head of Douglas Channel, a short drive from Kitimat. From Vancouver it is about 16 hours by road, so most people fly to the Northwest Regional Airport in Terrace, about an hour's drive away. Terrace is the nearest larger town and Prince Rupert is about 2.5 hours away.

The centre says it achieved full accreditation through Accreditation Canada's Qmentum site survey in November 2013. It is a member of the Association of BC First Nations Treatment Programs and, through that association, the National Native Addiction Partnership Foundation.

The centre has an Aftercare Coordinator on staff, and the intake process asks you to line up a referral worker who supports you before and after treatment. The last week of the 8-week program focuses on reflection, closure and planning for going home.
